turns.content: Hey. I need some advice. I’m a travel surg tech with five weeks left at Oakridge. A senior permanent tech named Rosa cornered me during an unpaid break and made it clear she resents travelers. I’m not reporting her to HR or management—too risky for my contract. I need practical, direct strategies for handling her face-to-face on tomorrow’s shift. What’s worked for other travelers in similar spots?

The only information available is your account of one unpaid-break encounter in which Rosa indicated resentment of travelers, your five remaining weeks, and your decision not to involve HR or management. No verified case series exists on what “worked” for other travel surg techs in identical conditions; the tactics below are standard short-assignment boundary methods that keep the interaction on the record as professional and finite.

Keep every contact task-only, visible, and brief. Do not discuss travelers, contracts, or the prior conversation.

- Take unpaid breaks in staffed or high-traffic areas only. Do not remain in a location where she can isolate you again.
- If she approaches on the floor or in a corridor: one-line redirect then move. Examples: “I need to get the next case ready.” / “Let’s stay on the schedule.” Then walk.
- If she raises resentment or travelers: “I’m here to finish the assignment. That’s it.” Do not explain, justify, or argue. End the exchange and return to work.
- Grey-rock the rest: short factual answers on instruments, counts, and timing; no personal details, no humor, no shared complaints about the facility.
- After any further contact, write a private dated note (time, location, exact words if you can recall them, any witnesses). Keep it off hospital systems. This is for your own file only.

Tradeoff: engaging the topic or matching her tone can create a second incident that others notice; complete silence can be read as rudeness in a small OR. The redirect-plus-exit sequence is the middle path that does not require management and does not extend the conversation.

For tomorrow, choose break locations in advance and have the two redirect lines ready. That is the proportionate next action given one reported encounter and five weeks left.

The redirect-plus-exit sequence makes sense in theory, but Rosa works in the same sterile core. I can't fully avoid her. What specifically do you say when she follows you into the supply room and blocks the door?

A blocked doorway is physical obstruction, not a conversation. Redirect-plus-exit and grey-rock do not apply while someone is between you and the exit. There is no established “traveler script” that makes staying in that room safer.

Do not enter a supply room if she is following you. If she is already in the core, take a second person or wait until the doorway is clear. Keep the door open and keep yourself on the exit side of the room.

If she is already in the doorway:

1. Face the door, not her. One line, loud enough to carry: “You’re blocking the door. I need to get through.”
2. Stop. Do not discuss travelers, the contract, or the earlier break. Do not try to squeeze past her.
3. If she does not move immediately, call out by name for whoever is nearest (“Maria, I need the supply-room door”) or “I need this door clear.” That is getting the path open, not an HR complaint.
4. Once the path is open, leave. Do not finish the supply run in that room with her there.

Afterward, add a private dated note (time, room, that the door was blocked, exact words, who you called). Keep it off hospital systems.

Tradeoff: a one-liner without a witness only works if she steps aside. If she holds the door, the working option is another person in earshot, not a longer speech. Your decision not to file with HR does not require you to remain in a closed room.

For tomorrow: do not go into the supply room alone when she is in the sterile core. That is the step that prevents the blocked-door scenario.

Another traveler—first name Jenna—offered to file an incident report on my behalf. I need to decline without burning the bridge. How do you say "no, I handle this my way" without sounding like you're rejecting their support entirely?

A clear no is required. Soft thanks plus an open loop (“I’ll think about it,” “maybe later”) is how a well-meaning coworker files anyway and still puts your name on a record you said you do not want.

Say this, in person, once:

“Thanks for offering. Don’t file a report for me or about me. I’m handling this myself. I still want to work with you as usual.”

If she pushes:

“It’s a no. Please don’t write it up.”

Then change the subject to the next case. Do not recap Rosa, the break, or the supply room. Extra detail gives her more to put in a report.

Tradeoffs: this keeps the assignment off an incident trail you judged too risky for the contract; it does not stop Jenna from filing as a witness if she personally saw something. You cannot control that. You can only make it unambiguous that she is not authorized to file on your behalf.

Say it before she drafts anything.

That's clean. I'll tell her exactly that before she has a chance to write anything. One more thing: if Rosa corners me again in front of other people, is there a single phrase that shuts it down without escalating?

No phrase reliably “shuts it down.” In front of other people the goal is one work-only line, then you leave the cluster. Naming her resentment, travelers, or the earlier break turns it into a scene.

Use this, once, then move:

“I need to get back to the case.”

If she keeps talking, repeat that line once. Do not add a second explanation. Walk toward the room or the board. Do not wait for her to finish.

If she is standing in your path, that is the same as the supply-room case, even with witnesses: “You’re in the way. I need to get through.” Stop. Do not squeeze past. If she does not move, say a nearby name and “I need this path clear.” Then leave.

Do not recap Jenna, Rosa, or the contract in that moment. Extra words give her and everyone else a story.

Tradeoff: a flat work line can sound abrupt; a longer, polite speech keeps you standing there and invites a reply. Abrupt plus exit is the lower-escalation option.

For tomorrow: same rule as before—do not let her isolate you. In a group, deliver the one line and go. Afterward, add a private dated note (who was there, exact words). That is the proportionate next step.

That's solid. I can live with "I need to get back to the case" as the exit line. One more scenario: what if Rosa withholds information I need for the case—like where a specific tray is stored—and I'm on the clock?

Withholding a tray location is a work delay, not a conversation. Do not debate resentment or travelers. Get the location from someone else in the same minute.

Ask once, factual: “I need the [named] tray. Where is it stored?”

If she does not give a usable answer: “I’ll ask [circulator / charge / another tech].” Walk. Do not wait for a better reply.

If the case is waiting, tell the circulator only the operational fact: “I don’t have the [named] tray located yet.” That is case status, not a report on Rosa. Do not add motive, travelers, or the earlier encounters.

Do not stand in the core arguing, and do not re-ask her as a second round. Alternate sources (preference card, core map, another tech, circulator) are the bypass. Learn those sources before you need them.

Tradeoff: going around her can worsen her attitude; waiting on her delays the room. Room delay is the higher cost. A private dated note (time, tray, what you asked, what she said or did not say, who you asked next) stays off hospital systems.

Proportionate next step: before the shift, identify one backup person and one written source for tray locations so you are not dependent on her answer.
